title: The browser, DOM and events
blurb: Events, bubbling, storage, the render pipeline, and what actually happens between typing a URL and seeing pixels.

questions.q: What is event bubbling?
choices: The event travels down from the document to the target and stops once it arrives
The event fires on the target, then on each of its children, from the outermost one inward
After firing on the target, the event travels up through each ancestor to the document
Every ancestor's listener runs first, and the target's own listener always runs last
questions.why: The full sequence is capture (document down to the target), the target itself, then bubble (target back up to the document). Listeners run in the bubble phase by default; the downward trip is capture, and you opt into it with `{ capture: true }`.
questions.asked: It underpins event delegation, which is the follow-up.

questions.q: Why attach one listener to the list like this rather than one to each row?
choices: It covers rows added later and needs one listener instead of hundreds
Row listeners never fire for clicks that land on a child span or button
Per-row listeners would each fire on every click anywhere in the list
`closest` stops propagation, so the page never sees clicks meant for rows
questions.why: Clicks bubble from the row to the list, so one listener handles every row, including ones rendered after page load, and `closest` finds which row was hit. A listener on a row does fire for clicks on its children, because they bubble to it; delegation wins on count and on rows added later.
questions.asked: A standard vanilla-JS question, and a good sign someone has built UI without a framework.

questions.q: What is the difference between `stopPropagation()` and `preventDefault()`?
choices: preventDefault stops the event reaching ancestors; stopPropagation cancels the default action
stopPropagation stops the event reaching other elements; preventDefault cancels the browser's action
preventDefault stops other listeners on the same element, whereas stopPropagation stops the ancestors
stopPropagation also cancels the default action, so a clicked link no longer navigates
questions.why: preventDefault stops the navigation, the form submit or the checkbox toggle; stopPropagation stops ancestors hearing about the event, and `stopImmediatePropagation` also skips other listeners on the same element. `return false` in a jQuery handler does both, which is why people confuse them; in a plain inline handler it only cancels the default.
questions.asked: Juniors mix these up constantly, and the jQuery `return false` habit is usually why.

questions.q: Which storage survives a browser restart and is scoped per origin?
choices: sessionStorage
an in-memory module variable
a cookie with no Expires or Max-Age
localStorage
questions.why: localStorage persists until it is cleared; sessionStorage lives only as long as the tab, and a cookie with no expiry is a session cookie. Both web storage APIs are per origin, synchronous, string-only and roughly 5 MB, and neither is sent to the server.
questions.asked: A quick check before the real follow-up: what you should and should not put there.

questions.q: Why is localStorage riskier than an HttpOnly cookie for holding an auth token?
choices: The browser attaches it to every request automatically, so a cross-site form can send it
Any script injected through XSS can read it; scripts cannot read an HttpOnly cookie
It is shared by every origin in the browser, so other sites can read it
It is wiped when the tab closes, so users must log in again far more often
questions.why: Anything in localStorage is one XSS bug away from being stolen. The trade-off: localStorage is immune to CSRF because nothing sends it automatically, while an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie resists theft but needs CSRF protection. Wiping on tab close is sessionStorage, not localStorage.
questions.asked: One of the most common frontend security questions. The wrong answer is 'localStorage is fine'.

questions.q: Why is this loop slow on a page with 500 cards?
choices: Each `style.height` write reflows and repaints the page before the next line runs
String concatenation in the loop creates 500 strings that trigger garbage collection
Each `offsetHeight` read forces a layout, because the previous write invalidated it
Setting inline styles makes the browser re-parse every stylesheet on the page
questions.why: Style writes are batched, but a geometry read such as `offsetHeight` makes the browser compute layout synchronously, mid-script, if anything changed. Alternating read and write forces one layout per card: layout thrashing. Read every height first, then write every height.
questions.asked: A frontend performance question that separates people who have profiled from people who have read about it.

questions.q: What does `defer` on a script tag do?
choices: Downloads in parallel, then runs after parsing finishes, in document order
Downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it arrives, in whatever order
Blocks the parser while it downloads, then runs before parsing resumes
Holds back the download itself until the page's load event has fired, then runs it
questions.why: `async` also downloads in parallel but runs the moment it lands, so order is not guaranteed: fine for analytics, wrong for app code with dependencies. No attribute at all blocks parsing. Deferred scripts run before `DOMContentLoaded`, not after `load`.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know why the script tag in your template can go in the head without blocking the page.

questions.q: What is the DOM, precisely?
choices: The HTML source text the server sent, which scripts then edit using ordinary string methods
The browser's rendering engine, which turns the HTML and CSS into pixels
A JavaScript library built into browsers that wraps the underlying HTML file
A live tree of objects built from the parsed HTML, which scripts can read and change
questions.why: The HTML is the input; the DOM is the live tree the browser builds from it and renders from. Changing the DOM does not change the HTML source, which is why 'view source' and devtools disagree.
questions.asked: A warm-up that shows whether you can separate source, tree and rendering.

questions.q: Why is 'state lives in data, not in the DOM' good advice?
choices: DOM reads are always slow, so keeping state in variables is mainly a speed win
Browsers reset element properties on every repaint, so any state you keep there is lost
Reading state back from the DOM couples logic to markup, so a markup change breaks it
It only matters in React, where direct DOM edits are overwritten on each render
questions.why: If the truth is `todos`, rendering is a pure function of it and any bug is in one place. If the truth is 'whatever the list element shows', every feature re-derives it and a formatting change becomes a logic bug. Speed is a side benefit, and the advice holds in vanilla JS too.
questions.asked: It is the single idea that makes React make sense, so it comes up in frontend interviews constantly.

questions.q: What is a debounce?
choices: Run at most once every N ms, however often it is called
Wait until N ms after the last call, then run once
Run immediately, then ignore further calls for N ms
Queue every call and run them one by one N ms apart
questions.why: Debounce collapses a burst into one trailing call, which suits a search box. Running at most once every N ms is throttle, which suits scroll or resize handlers that need steady updates.
questions.asked: Nearly universal. Be ready to write both from scratch.

questions.q: How does `event.target` differ from `event.currentTarget`?
choices: `target` is where the event started; `currentTarget` is the element whose listener runs
`target` is the element with the listener; `currentTarget` is the element that was clicked
`currentTarget` is always `document`, since every event finally lands there
`target` is the parent of the clicked element; `currentTarget` is the element
questions.why: In a delegated handler, `currentTarget` is the container the listener sits on and `target` is the deep descendant that received the click. Swapping them is the classic delegation bug: `target` may be a span inside the row, not the row.
questions.asked: It usually comes straight after event delegation, as the detail that makes delegation work.

questions.q: What is CORS actually enforcing?
choices: The server refusing cross-origin requests before its route handler ever gets to run
The browser encrypting cross-origin traffic so that other sites on the network cannot intercept it
A network firewall rule that blocks requests arriving from unrecognised domains
The browser withholding a cross-origin response from your script unless the server allows it
questions.why: A simple request often reaches the server and runs; the browser then hides the response from your JavaScript because `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is missing. That is why you fix CORS on the server, and why curl or Postman never hit it.
questions.asked: Universally asked, and the tell is whether you say 'the server has to send the header'.

questions.q: What makes the browser send a CORS preflight before a cross-origin request?
choices: Every cross-origin request, so the browser can check the server's policy first
Only requests sent with `credentials: 'include'`, so cookies can be checked
A method other than GET/HEAD/POST, a non-safelisted header, or a JSON Content-Type
Any cross-origin POST or PUT, whatever headers and Content-Type it carries
questions.why: Simple requests (GET, HEAD, or POST with a form-style Content-Type and safelisted headers) go straight out. Anything else gets an OPTIONS request first, and your server has to answer it: a 404 or 401 on OPTIONS is the most common "CORS is broken" cause. Cookies alone do not trigger a preflight.
questions.asked: It explains why adding an Authorization header or JSON body suddenly breaks a call that worked.

questions.q: What is the difference between `innerHTML` and `textContent`?
choices: textContent is faster but otherwise identical; both render any tags inside the string
innerHTML parses the string as HTML, so user input can inject markup; textContent cannot
innerHTML escapes `<script>` tags, so it is safe for user input, unlike textContent
textContent strips whitespace and newlines, while innerHTML keeps the string as written
questions.why: Assigning unsanitised input to innerHTML lets an attacker inject markup. Inserted `
questions.asked: The most direct XSS question there is.

questions.q: Which order best describes what happens between typing a URL and seeing the page?
choices: The HTTP request, then DNS to find the server, then TLS, then layout and paint
DNS and TLS, the HTTP request, then all scripts run before any DOM is built
DNS, the HTTP request, then paint the raw HTML before any CSS is downloaded
DNS, TCP and TLS, the HTTP request, then DOM and CSSOM, layout and paint
questions.why: You must resolve the name before you can connect, and connect (TCP, then TLS) before you can send the request. The parser builds the DOM as HTML streams in, CSS becomes the CSSOM, and layout and paint follow. Scripts run during parsing, not before it, and CSS blocks first paint.
questions.asked: A classic open-ended question; interviewers use it to see how deep your mental model goes.

questions.q: Clicking Clear also submits the search form. Why?
questions.code:
<form action="/search">
  <input name="q">
  <button onclick="clearField()">Clear</button>
</form>
choices: A `<button>` with no `type` attribute defaults to `type="submit"`
The click event bubbles to the `<form>`, and forms submit on any click
`clearField` returns undefined, which an inline handler treats as submit
Every clickable element inside a `<form>` submits it unless disabled
questions.why: Inside a form, a button with no `type` is a submit button, so its click triggers submission after `clearField` runs. Add `type="button"` for buttons that only run JavaScript. Bubbling is not the cause: clicks on a plain `<div>` bubble to the form and submit nothing.
questions.asked: The classic 'my page reloads when I click the button' bug, in React and vanilla JS alike.

questions.q: What is a memory leak in a browser app, most commonly?
choices: Creating many short-lived objects in a loop faster than GC can collect them
Holding a large array in a `const`, so the engine can never reassign or free it
Listeners, timers or observers never removed, which keep detached nodes reachable
Fetching large JSON responses, which the browser caches in memory for the session
questions.why: A detached DOM node still referenced by a live listener, interval or observer cannot be collected. Short-lived objects are what the garbage collector handles best, and `const` stops reassignment, not collection. This is exactly what a React effect cleanup exists to prevent.
questions.asked: It connects straight to 'why does useEffect need a cleanup?'

questions.q: What does `requestAnimationFrame` give you over `setTimeout` for animation?
choices: The callback runs on the compositor thread, so heavy work in it cannot block the page
The callback runs just before the next repaint, in step with the display, and pauses in hidden tabs
The callback runs exactly every 16 ms whatever the display refresh rate, so animations stay precise
The callback runs before pending microtasks, so it beats any promise callback queued
questions.why: Animating with setTimeout runs at a rate unrelated to the display, causing dropped or doubled frames and wasted work. rAF runs once per frame at the display rate, which may be 60, 120 or 144 Hz, on the main thread, and stops while the tab is hidden.
questions.asked: It shows whether you have animated anything by hand, and leads into why layout reads belong in rAF.

questions.q: What are the cookie attributes `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite` for?
choices: Encrypt its value, send it only over HTTPS, and expire it after the session
Hide it from JavaScript, compress it in transit, and bind it to a single tab
Sign its value, send it only on the same path, and block third-party reads
Hide it from JavaScript, send it only over HTTPS, and limit cross-site sending
questions.why: HttpOnly blocks theft by XSS, Secure blocks interception over plain HTTP, and `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` is the main defence against CSRF. None of them encrypts or signs the value; that is the server's job. Session cookies should carry all three.
questions.asked: A guaranteed follow-up to any auth question.

questions.q: What does adding `type="module"` to a `<script>` change?
choices: It is deferred by default, runs in strict mode and gets its own module scope
It runs before any classic scripts, so it can set up globals they depend on
It is only a bundler hint; browsers run it exactly like a classic script
It runs on a separate thread, like a worker, so it cannot touch the DOM
questions.why: Module scripts are deferred, always strict, do not leak top-level declarations onto `window`, can use `import`/`export`, and are fetched with CORS. That is why `this` is undefined at the top level of a module but `window` in a classic script. They run on the main thread with full DOM access.
questions.asked: Relevant the moment you ship without a bundler, or debug why a global is suddenly undefined.

questions.q: Why does a page feel janky while JavaScript is busy?
choices: The browser pauses the GPU while scripts run, so frames cannot be composited
The browser throttles every script on the page once any one runs over 50 ms
JavaScript and rendering share the main thread, so a long task delays paint and input
CSS animations and transitions all freeze whenever a script is executing
questions.why: Anything over about 50 ms is a long task and delays the next frame and the response to input. Compositor-only animations (transform, opacity) can keep running, which is why they feel smoother. The fixes: do less, split the work into chunks, or move it to a Web Worker.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know there is one main thread and what competes for it.

questions.q: Four elements have the class `item`. How many still have it after this loop?
choices: None: the loop visits each of the four elements once and removes the class
Two: the live collection shrinks as you go, so every other one is skipped
One: the last element is skipped because `length` is read only at the start
None, but the loop throws once the collection length changes under it
questions.why: `getElementsByClassName` returns a live HTMLCollection, so removing the class drops the element from it and the next one slides into the current index. `querySelectorAll` returns a static NodeList and would visit all four. `length` is re-read on every iteration.
questions.asked: It shows whether you know which DOM methods return live collections, a bug that only appears with real data.

questions.q: In a browser, which statement about these listener options is true?
choices: `ac.abort()` removes the wheel listener without a reference to `onWheel`
`passive: true` runs `onWheel` off the main thread so it cannot delay scrolling
`passive: true` makes a `preventDefault()` in `onWheel` cancel the scroll sooner
`once: true` removes `onClose` only after it has returned without throwing
questions.why: `signal` ties a listener to an AbortController, so one `abort()` removes every listener registered with it. `passive` promises you will not call `preventDefault`, so scrolling need not wait for the handler; it still runs on the main thread and a `preventDefault` is ignored. `once` removes the listener before it is invoked, even if it throws.
questions.asked: It checks modern listener hygiene: cleanup without keeping handler references, and scroll handlers that do not block.

questions.q: Why prefer this to a `scroll` listener that checks `sentinel.getBoundingClientRect()`?
choices: The observer callback runs on a separate thread, so its work never touches the main thread at all
A scroll listener cannot read element positions without first calling rAF
The observer fires synchronously on every scroll event, so it never misses a frame
The browser tracks visibility itself, so no code runs per scroll event and no layout is forced
questions.why: The browser computes intersections as part of its rendering steps and calls you only when visibility crosses the threshold, here 200 px early. A scroll handler runs on every scroll event and each `getBoundingClientRect` can force layout. The callback still runs on the main thread, asynchronously.
questions.asked: Infinite scroll and lazy loading come up in every frontend role, and this is the modern way to build them.

questions.q: Tabs A and B on the same origin both run this. Tab A runs the last line. Where does `showLoggedOut` run?
choices: In both tabs, because each of them has registered a listener for the event
Only in tab B: the event fires in other same-origin tabs, not the one that wrote
Only in tab A, because storage events are scoped to the tab that made the change
In neither tab: `removeItem` does not fire the event, only `setItem` does
questions.why: The `storage` event is delivered to other documents of the same origin, never to the one that made the change, and `removeItem` fires it with `newValue` null. Tab A must update its own UI directly. `BroadcastChannel` is the purpose-built alternative and likewise does not echo a message back to the channel that posted it.
questions.asked: Logging out everywhere at once is a real product requirement, and the self-exclusion detail catches most people.

questions.q: In a hand-rolled router using this code, when does `popstate` fire?
questions.code:
history.pushState({ page: 2 }, '', '?page=2');
window.addEventListener('popstate', (e) => render(e.state));
choices: Straight after every `pushState` call, so the app can render the new URL
Only when a full page reload lands on a URL that was added with `pushState`
When the user goes back or forward, not when `pushState` itself is called
On any URL change the app makes, including each call to `replaceState`
questions.why: `pushState` changes the URL and adds a history entry without loading anything or firing `popstate`, so the app must render the new view itself. `popstate` fires on back/forward navigation with the saved state. The server must also answer `?page=2` on a reload, because `pushState` never asked it.
questions.asked: It shows whether you understand what a client-side router does under the hood, and why deep links need server support.

questions.q: What is the difference between `DOMContentLoaded` and `load`?
choices: DOMContentLoaded waits for images and styles; load fires as soon as HTML is parsed
DOMContentLoaded fires before deferred scripts run; load fires only after they have all run
DOMContentLoaded fires after the first paint; load fires before anything is painted
DOMContentLoaded fires once the HTML is parsed; load also waits for images and styles
questions.why: `DOMContentLoaded` fires when the document is parsed and deferred scripts have run, so the DOM is ready to query. `load` waits for subresources such as images, stylesheets and iframes. Code that only needs the DOM should use the earlier event, or simply a deferred or module script.
questions.asked: A junior screening staple, and a way into how deferred scripts remove the need for either event.

questions.q: A keyboard shortcut handler calls form.submit() on a form whose required fields are empty. The form also has a submit listener that calls preventDefault() and posts with fetch. What happens?
choices: The browser shows its validation bubbles on the empty fields and sends nothing
The submit listener runs and posts the empty fields with fetch, skipping validation
The page navigates: submit() skips constraint validation and fires no submit event
It throws an InvalidStateError, because submit() is refused while a field is invalid
questions.why: form.submit() is the legacy imperative path: it runs no constraint validation and does not dispatch a submit event, so your listener never sees it and the browser performs a full-page form navigation with the empty values. form.requestSubmit() behaves like clicking the submit button: it validates, fires submit, and lets preventDefault take over, which is what an SPA wants.
questions.asked: A real 'why did my SPA reload the page' bug; knowing requestSubmit exists and why it differs from submit is a mid-level tell.

questions.q: You want to send a small 'session ended' beacon when the user leaves the page, including on mobile where tabs are killed in the background. Which approach is most reliable?
choices: An `unload` listener that calls `fetch` with `await`, so the request finishes before the page goes
A `beforeunload` listener that returns a string, which keeps the page open until the send completes
A `visibilitychange` listener that calls `navigator.sendBeacon` when the state becomes hidden
A synchronous `XMLHttpRequest` in `unload`, since browsers are required to complete those
questions.why: `visibilitychange` to `hidden` is the last event mobile browsers reliably fire before discarding a page, and `sendBeacon` (or `fetch` with `keepalive: true`) hands the request to the browser so it completes after the page is gone. `unload` often does not fire on mobile and blocks the back/forward cache; `beforeunload` exists to ask the user whether to leave, not to delay it; synchronous XHR in unload is deprecated and ignored by modern Chrome.
questions.asked: Analytics and autosave both hit this, and naming `sendBeacon` plus the reason `unload` is unreliable shows real mobile experience.

questions.q: In a current browser, the user clicks the `<span>` inside `#btn`, which sits inside `#outer`. In what order do the logs appear?
choices: outer bubble, outer capture, btn bubble, btn capture
btn bubble, btn capture, outer capture, outer bubble
outer capture, btn capture, btn bubble, outer bubble
outer capture, btn bubble, btn capture, outer bubble
questions.why: Capture runs from the window down to the target, then bubble runs back up, so `#outer` capture comes first and `#outer` bubble last. `#btn` is an ancestor of the real target (the span), so its capture listener runs on the way down; even on the target itself, current browsers run capture listeners before bubble ones rather than in registration order.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see whether you know the three phases as a sequence, not just the word "bubbling".

questions.q: Two listeners are on the same button, and the body also listens for clicks. What runs when the button is clicked?
choices: A and B, but not body, since only bubbling to ancestors is stopped
Only A: later listeners on the button and all ancestors are skipped
A and body, since only listeners on the same element are skipped
A, B and body, since the call only affects the default action
questions.why: `stopImmediatePropagation` stops the event reaching any ancestor and also skips the remaining listeners on the current element. Plain `stopPropagation` is the one that lets B run and only blocks the trip to the body; neither touches the default action, which is `preventDefault`'s job.
questions.asked: It separates people who have debugged a third-party widget swallowing clicks from people who only know `stopPropagation`.

questions.q: How many times does `onClick` run when the button is clicked once?
choices: Three times, once for each call
Twice
Once, as duplicates are always dropped
Four times
questions.why: A listener is identified by type, callback and the capture flag. The second bubble-phase registration is a duplicate and ignored, but the capture registration is a distinct listener, so the function runs twice. Other options such as `once` or `passive` do not form part of that identity.
questions.asked: It explains a class of "handler fires twice" bugs and why the capture flag matters when removing listeners.

questions.q: Why does the button still log after the cleanup code runs?
choices: Listeners can only be removed with an AbortController signal
The second arrow is a different function, so nothing matches it
Arrow functions are bound at creation and so can never be removed
Removal only takes effect after the next click has been dispatched
questions.why: `removeEventListener` looks for the exact same function reference, and two identical-looking arrows are two separate objects. Keep the handler in a variable, or register with `{ signal }` and abort the controller; arrows are removable like any function when you hold the reference.
questions.asked: A common leak and duplicate-handler bug in vanilla code and in React effects that clean up by hand.

questions.q: After this runs, does clicking the button still call `track`?
questions.code:
btn.addEventListener('click', track, true);
btn.removeEventListener('click', track);
choices: No: removal matches on the type and the function only
No, but only because the capture listener never fired on the target
Yes: the removal targeted a bubble listener that did not exist
It throws, since there is no bubble listener to remove
questions.why: The capture flag is part of a listener's identity, so removing without `true` looks for a bubble-phase `track`, finds none, and silently does nothing. Pass the same `capture` value to remove it; `removeEventListener` never throws for a missing listener.
questions.asked: The silent no-op is what makes this nasty; it shows up in libraries that add capture listeners and "clean up" wrongly.

questions.q: Inside a handler registered as `btn.addEventListener('click', handler)`, what is `this`?
questions.code:
function handler() { this.classList.add('done'); }
const arrow = () => { this.classList.add('done'); };
choices: `btn` for `handler`; for `arrow`, whatever `this` was where it was defined
`btn` in both, as `addEventListener` binds every callback to the element
`window` for `handler`; for `arrow`, the element it was attached to
`event.target` for both, the innermost element that was clicked
questions.why: A regular function listener is called with `this` set to `currentTarget`, the element the listener is on. Arrow functions have no `this` of their own and capture it lexically, so at module top level it is `undefined`. Using `e.currentTarget` avoids relying on either.
questions.asked: It checks that you know arrow functions change `this`, which interviewers probe in event-handler form.

questions.q: The delete button contains an SVG icon. Clicking the icon logs `undefined`, but clicking the button's padding logs the id. Why?
questions.code:
<button class="delete" data-id="42"><svg>…</svg></button>
<script>
table.addEventListener('click', (e) => console.log(e.target.dataset.id));
</script>
choices: SVG elements do not support `dataset`, so the lookup throws and logs nothing
`e.target` is the icon element that was hit, which has no `data-id` of its own
The icon swallows the click, so the table receives a synthetic copy of the event
Delegated listeners always report the deepest element, which is the document
questions.why: `target` is the innermost element under the pointer, here the `<svg>` or its `<path>`. Use `e.target.closest('[data-id]')` to walk up to the element you care about. The icon does not swallow anything; the event bubbles normally with the icon as target.
questions.asked: Every delegated-listener implementation hits this in the first week, so it is a quick practical check.

questions.q: A form-level listener should highlight whichever field currently has focus. Which listener works?
choices: `form.addEventListener('focus', …)`, as focus bubbles like click does
`form.addEventListener('focusin', …)`, since `focusin` bubbles
`form.addEventListener('focus', …, { passive: true })`
`form.addEventListener('change', …)`, which fires on focus
questions.why: `focus` and `blur` do not bubble, so a listener on the form never hears them from its fields. `focusin` and `focusout` are the bubbling equivalents; registering `focus` with `capture: true` would also work. `change` fires when a committed value changes, not on focus.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know delegation has exceptions, which is the natural follow-up after explaining it.

questions.q: You delegate hover effects from a large list. Why does `mouseenter` on the list not tell you which row the pointer entered?
choices: `mouseenter` only fires on touch devices, so desktop needs `pointerover`
`mouseenter` fires only when the list itself is entered, since it does not bubble
`mouseenter` fires on the document, never on elements inside a scroll container
`mouseenter` reports the row in `relatedTarget`, which the handler must read
questions.why: `mouseenter`/`mouseleave` do not bubble and fire only when the pointer crosses that element's own boundary. `mouseover`/`mouseout` (or `pointerover`/`pointerout`) bubble, so a list listener sees every row, with `closest` to find the row and `relatedTarget` to ignore moves within it.
questions.asked: Hover delegation is less common than click delegation, so this checks real understanding of which events bubble.

questions.q: A child component fires this, and a listener on an ancestor `<section>` never runs. Why?
choices: Custom event names must not contain a hyphen, so it is dropped
Custom events need `bubbles: true`, which defaults to false
`detail` is only readable by listeners on the dispatching element
Only trusted events reach ancestors, and this one is synthetic
questions.why: Events built with `new Event` or `new CustomEvent` default to `bubbles: false`, so only listeners on the dispatching element run. Add `bubbles: true` (and `composed: true` to cross a shadow root). Synthetic events bubble fine once asked; `isTrusted` is false but propagation is unaffected.
questions.asked: A standard building block for component communication without a framework, and the default catches people out.

questions.q: What is logged, and in what order?
choices: before, after, handler: dispatch queues a task for its listeners
before, after, handler: listeners run as microtasks after this code
before, handler, after: `dispatchEvent` calls listeners synchronously
handler, before, after: listeners registered first run first
questions.why: `dispatchEvent` runs every listener synchronously before it returns, and its return value tells you whether any of them called `preventDefault`. Browser-generated events arrive as tasks, but a dispatch from your own code is an ordinary nested call.
questions.asked: It shows whether you can reason about synchronous event dispatch when building or testing your own event emitters.

questions.q: A listener checks `event.isTrusted`. When is it `false`?
choices: When the event came from a keyboard rather than from a pointer device
When the page is embedded in a cross-origin iframe
When the listener was added with `{ passive: true }`
When script created it with `new Event()` and `dispatchEvent`
questions.why: `isTrusted` is true only for events the browser generated from real user or system activity; events your code constructs and dispatches, and the click fired by `el.click()`, are untrusted. Browsers use it to gate things such as popups, and analytics or anti-bot code can check it.
questions.asked: It comes up when explaining why a scripted click cannot open a popup or trigger fullscreen.

questions.q: Two listeners on one button each queue a microtask. What order do the logs appear in when a real user clicks, and when code calls `btn.click()`?
choices: The same in both: listener 1, listener 2, micro 1, micro 2
User: listener 1, micro 1, listener 2, micro 2; `click()`: both listeners first
User: both listeners first; `click()`: listener 1, micro 1, listener 2, micro 2
The same in both: listener 1, micro 1, listener 2, micro 2
questions.why: Microtasks run whenever the JavaScript stack empties. For a real click the browser calls each listener from native code, so the stack empties between them and each microtask runs straight after its listener. With `btn.click()` your script is still on the stack, so both listeners run before any microtask.
questions.asked: A deep event-loop question that also explains why tests that call `click()` can order effects differently from real users.

questions.q: A keyboard shortcut should be Ctrl+Z for undo on every keyboard layout, including AZERTY. What should the handler compare?
choices: `e.code === 'KeyZ'`, the physical key position, whatever the layout
`e.key === 'z'`, the character the key produces on this layout
`e.keyCode === 90`, which is layout-independent and standard
`e.which === 26`, the control character that Ctrl+Z produces
questions.why: `key` is the character the user's layout produces, so it matches the letter Z printed on the key; that is what shortcuts labelled by letter should use. `code` is the physical position, which on AZERTY is where W is, so it suits games (WASD) rather than letter shortcuts. `keyCode` and `which` are deprecated.
questions.asked: Checks that you use the modern KeyboardEvent properties and know the difference, which matters for international users.

questions.q: A search box should filter as the user types, including on paste and on mobile autocorrect. Which event fits?
choices: `keyup`, which fires after each key is released on the field
`input`, which fires whenever the value changes by any means
`change`, which fires as each character is typed into the field
`keypress`, which fires once for every character that is entered
questions.why: `input` fires on every value change: typing, paste, cut, drag-drop, IME and autocorrect. `change` on a text field fires only when the edited value is committed, usually on blur. Key events miss paste from menus and autocorrect, and `keypress` is deprecated.
questions.asked: A quick junior check that pairs naturally with a debounce follow-up.

questions.q: A slider thumb is dragged with pointer events. When the pointer leaves the thumb mid-drag, `pointermove` stops arriving. What fixes it?
choices: Use `mousemove`, which keeps firing on the thumb outside its bounds
Call `thumb.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId)` in the `pointerdown` handler
Add `{ passive: true }` so moves are delivered off the main thread
Call `e.preventDefault()` in `pointermove` so the drag is not cancelled
questions.why: Pointer capture retargets all later events for that pointer to the thumb until `pointerup`, even when the pointer is over something else or outside the window. Mouse events have no such behaviour, which is why old code attached move listeners to `document`. For touch, `touch-action: none` on the thumb stops the browser scrolling instead.
questions.asked: Drag interactions come up in kanban and slider tasks, and pointer capture is the clean answer.

questions.q: Which code gives the "You have unsaved changes" prompt when the user tries to close a tab with a dirty form?
choices: It works: browsers show a generic prompt when `preventDefault` is called
It fails: the handler must return the custom message text to display
It fails: `beforeunload` only fires when navigating links, not closing tabs
It works, and the browser shows the text from the form's `title` field
questions.why: Calling `preventDefault` (or setting `returnValue`) asks the browser to confirm; browsers show their own generic wording and ignore custom strings. Some also require the user to have interacted with the page. Add the listener only while the form is dirty, because a permanent `beforeunload` listener can hurt the back/forward cache.
questions.asked: A common product request; strong answers mention that the message is not customisable and the listener should be conditional.

questions.q: What does clicking the button do?
choices: Logs 2, 3, 4
Logs 2 only
Logs 3, 4, then 2
questions.why: An `on…` property holds one handler, so the second assignment replaces the first; it takes part in dispatch as a listener registered at the point it was first set. `addEventListener` adds independent listeners, which is why libraries use it: they cannot clobber each other.
questions.asked: A basic check that explains why `addEventListener` is the default in shared code.

questions.q: A page adds `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'`. Which existing code stops working?
choices: `<script src="/app.js" defer>`, since deferred scripts need a nonce
`btn.addEventListener('click', save)` inside `/app.js`
`<button onclick="save()">Save</button>` in the HTML
`import { save } from './save.js'` inside a module script
questions.why: Inline event-handler attributes are inline script, and a `script-src` without `'unsafe-inline'` (or a matching hash with `'unsafe-hashes'`) blocks them. Scripts loaded from the same origin and listeners attached from them are allowed. This is one practical reason to keep handlers out of markup.
questions.asked: Links event handling to CSP, which interviewers like because it shows the security reason behind a style rule.

questions.q: A delegated handler on a nested menu finds the clicked item like this. When can it act on the wrong element?
choices: When `menu` itself sits inside an element with `data-action`
When the clicked element is a text node rather than an element
When the item has children, as `closest` stops at the first child
When two items share an action, as `closest` returns the first one
questions.why: `closest` walks all the way up to the document, so a click on menu padding can match an ancestor outside the menu that happens to have `data-action`. Guard with `if (item && menu.contains(item))`. `e.target` is always an element for clicks, and `closest` walks up, never down.
questions.asked: A strong delegation answer includes the containment check; it is the difference between a demo and production code.

questions.q: This module script runs after the page has loaded. Why does `init` never run?
questions.code:
// loaded later via dynamic import()
document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init);
choices: `DOMContentLoaded` only fires for listeners on `window`, not `document`
The event has already fired, and late listeners do not get a replay
Module scripts cannot listen for document lifecycle events at all
The listener needs `{ once: true }` to be allowed after parsing
questions.why: Events are not sticky: a listener added after `DOMContentLoaded` has fired simply waits for an event that never comes. Check `document.readyState` first (`'loading'` means wait, otherwise run now), or rely on deferred and module scripts, which already run after parsing.
questions.asked: It catches widgets that work in a static page but break when loaded lazily.

questions.q: What does this log?
questions.why: `childNodes` includes every node, and the whitespace between tags becomes three text nodes around the two `<li>` elements, making five. `children` contains only elements. The same trap makes `firstChild` return a text node where you expected the first `<li>`; use `firstElementChild`.
questions.asked: A small but real source of "undefined is not a function" bugs when walking the DOM.

questions.q: A list of 200 rows is rendered with this loop. Apart from speed, what breaks?
choices: Nothing: `+=` appends new markup after the existing rows
Only the final row renders, since each assignment replaces the list
The rows appear in reverse order, as each string is prepended
Existing rows are rebuilt each time, losing listeners and input state
questions.why: `innerHTML +=` reads the whole list back as a string, appends, and reparses it, so every existing `<li>` is destroyed and recreated each time. Listeners on them, focus and typed values are lost, and the work is quadratic. Build nodes with `createElement` and `append`, or use `insertAdjacentHTML('beforeend', …)`, which does not touch existing children.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know what `innerHTML` really does, beyond "it can be an XSS risk".

questions.q: What does a `<template>` element give you when rendering repeated rows?
choices: Parsed but inert markup: nothing renders, loads or runs until you clone it
A string of HTML that is reparsed and sanitised each time you clone it
Markup that renders hidden and updates each clone when it is changed
A reusable custom element whose instances share one shadow root
questions.why: `<template>` content is parsed once into a `DocumentFragment` that is not rendered, and its images do not load and scripts do not run. `content.cloneNode(true)` copies it cheaply for each row; clones are independent, and nothing about it sanitises user data, so fill it with `textContent`.
questions.asked: Framework-free rendering questions often end here, and it links to web components.

questions.q: Why can reading `el.innerText` inside a loop be much slower than reading `el.textContent`?
choices: `innerText` decodes HTML entities, which requires parsing the markup again
`innerText` is CSS-aware, so it must lay out the page to know what is visible
`innerText` walks shadow roots too, while `textContent` stops at their hosts
`innerText` is computed asynchronously and blocks until the next frame
questions.why: `innerText` returns the text as rendered: it skips `display: none` content and applies line breaks from layout, so reading it can force a synchronous style and layout. `textContent` returns the raw text of all descendant nodes with no layout. Neither parses or touches shadow roots.
questions.asked: It shows you know the two are not synonyms, one being layout-dependent.

questions.q: The element is `<div data-user-id="7">`. What is `el.dataset.userId`?
choices: The number `7`
The string `"7"`
`undefined`, as the key must be `user-id`
`null` until the element is attached
questions.why: `data-*` attributes map to camelCased `dataset` keys, so `data-user-id` becomes `userId`, and attribute values are always strings. Convert with `Number(el.dataset.userId)` when you need a number; writing `dataset.userId = 8` updates the attribute to `"8"`.
questions.asked: A small but frequent source of `"7" === 7` bugs in delegated handlers.

questions.q: The input was rendered as `<input name="qty" value="1">`, and the user has typed 5. What do these return?
questions.why: The `value` attribute is the initial value and is reflected by `defaultValue`; typing changes only the `value` property. That is why `form.reset()` goes back to "1" and why selectors like `[value="5"]` do not match typed text. Checkboxes have the same split between `checked` and `defaultChecked`.
questions.asked: The attribute-versus-property distinction explains many DOM bugs and how frameworks decide what to set.

questions.q: What does `btn.disabled` return after this line?
questions.code: btn.setAttribute('disabled', 'false');
choices: `false`, since the attribute value is the string "false"
`true`, because a boolean attribute is on whenever present
`"false"`, the attribute value as a string
It throws, since only "" or "disabled" are allowed
questions.why: For boolean attributes such as `disabled`, `checked` and `hidden`, presence means true whatever the value. Use `btn.disabled = false` or `removeAttribute('disabled')`, or `toggleAttribute('disabled', cond)`.
questions.asked: A classic bug from string-building markup, and a quick check of how HTML attributes really work.

questions.q: What does `el.classList.toggle('open', isOpen)` do?
choices: Flips `open`, then returns whether it matches `isOpen`
Adds `open` if `isOpen` is truthy and removes it otherwise
Flips `open` only when `isOpen` is true, and otherwise does nothing
Sets the whole `className` to `open` or to an empty string
questions.why: The optional second argument turns `toggle` into a conditional add/remove, which is what state-driven rendering needs: the class always matches the state, however many times it runs. Without it, `toggle` flips the class and returns whether it is now present.
questions.asked: It shows the habit of deriving the DOM from state rather than flipping it, a theme interviewers probe.

questions.q: You clone a row that has a click listener attached with `addEventListener`. What happens when the clone is clicked?
questions.code:
const copy = row.cloneNode(true);
table.append(copy);
choices: The listener runs, since a deep clone copies listeners on every node
The listener runs only if it was added with the `capture` option
Nothing, as `addEventListener` listeners are not copied by cloning
The listener runs twice, once for the original and once for the copy
questions.why: `cloneNode` copies attributes and, when deep, child nodes, but not listeners registered with `addEventListener`. Inline `onclick` attributes do get copied, being attributes. This is another reason delegation suits dynamic lists: new rows need no wiring.
questions.asked: It connects cloning to delegation, which interviewers use to see if you design for dynamic content.

questions.q: You need an element's position relative to the whole document, to scroll there later. What do you compute?
choices: `el.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY`
`el.getBoundingClientRect().top`, already document-relative
`el.offsetTop`, always measured from the top of the document
`el.scrollTop`, the distance scrolled to reach the element
questions.why: `getBoundingClientRect` is relative to the viewport, so add the current scroll offset to get a document coordinate. `offsetTop` is relative to the `offsetParent`, which is the document only when no ancestor is positioned, and `scrollTop` is how far the element's own content is scrolled.
questions.asked: Tooltips, scroll-to and sticky UI all need this, and mixing up the coordinate systems is common.

questions.q: A scrollable log panel should auto-scroll only when the user is already at the bottom. Which check is right?
choices: `panel.scrollTop === panel.offsetHeight - panel.clientTop`
`panel.scrollHeight - panel.scrollTop - panel.clientHeight < 2`
`panel.scrollTop + panel.offsetWidth >= panel.scrollWidth`
`panel.getBoundingClientRect().bottom === window.innerHeight`
questions.why: `scrollHeight` is the full content height, `clientHeight` the visible inner height and `scrollTop` how far it has scrolled, so their difference is the distance left to the bottom. A small tolerance absorbs fractional pixels on zoomed or high-DPI screens. `offsetHeight` includes borders and scrollbars.
questions.asked: A real chat or log feature; knowing the three size properties is what makes the answer quick.

questions.q: How many times does the observer callback run, and when?
choices: Three times, synchronously, before "done" each time with 1
Once, after "done", with 3 records, as a microtask
Once, on the next animation frame, with 3 records
Three times, after "done", each run with a single record
questions.why: Mutation observers batch records and deliver them in a microtask after the current script finishes, so the three appends arrive together in one call after "done". They replaced the synchronous, slow mutation events, which are deprecated and already removed from Chrome.
questions.asked: It tests the batching model, which matters when an observer reacts to DOM changes made by a framework.

questions.q: A chart must redraw when its container changes width, including when a sidebar collapses. Which API fits?
choices: A `window` `resize` listener that reads the container width
A `ResizeObserver` watching the container element
A `MutationObserver` on the container's `style` attribute
An `IntersectionObserver` with a threshold of 1.0
questions.why: Collapsing a sidebar changes the container's size without resizing the window, so a `resize` listener misses it. `ResizeObserver` reports size changes of the element itself, whatever caused them, and delivers them once per frame after layout. A `MutationObserver` sees attribute changes, not layout results.
questions.asked: Dashboards and responsive widgets need this, and it shows you think in components rather than the window.

questions.q: A page has `<div id="config">`, and a legacy script reads a global `config` that someone forgot to define. What happens?
choices: It throws a ReferenceError, because `config` was never declared
`config` is the div element, so the check passes with the wrong value
`config` is `undefined`, so the block is skipped silently
It reads `document.config`, which is `null` in standards mode
questions.why: Browsers expose elements with an `id` as named properties of `window`, so an undeclared `config` resolves to the element instead of throwing. The code then runs with a DOM node as its settings. Modules and bundled code avoid most of this, but it still bites global scripts and tests.
questions.asked: An obscure but real legacy bug; recognising it signals deep debugging experience.

questions.q: What is `total` after this runs in a browser?
questions.code:
localStorage.setItem('count', 5);
const total = localStorage.getItem('count') + 1;
choices: `NaN`
A TypeError
questions.why: Web Storage keeps only strings, so the 5 is stored as "5" and `getItem` returns "5"; `+ 1` then concatenates. Parse on the way out (`Number(...)`), or store JSON and `JSON.parse` it. `getItem` also returns `null` for a missing key, which needs its own default.
questions.asked: A first-week bug that shows whether you know the storage API is string-only.

questions.q: A settings object is saved with `localStorage.setItem('prefs', prefs)`. What is stored?
choices: A structured clone of the object, as IndexedDB would store it
A JSON string of the object, serialised automatically on save
A reference that is lost when the tab closes, like a variable
The literal string `"[object Object]"`
questions.why: The value is converted with `String()`, which for a plain object gives "[object Object]", so the data is gone. Use `JSON.stringify` to save and `JSON.parse` to load, and remember Dates come back as strings and Maps and Sets as `{}`.
questions.asked: It checks that you serialise explicitly and know what JSON loses on the round trip.

questions.q: A wizard keeps its progress in `sessionStorage`. The user opens the app in a second tab by typing the URL. What does that tab see?
choices: The same progress, since session storage is shared per origin
The same progress until either tab writes, then a separate copy
An empty store, since session storage belongs to one tab
An empty store, until the first tab is closed or reloaded
questions.why: `sessionStorage` is scoped to one top-level browsing context (a tab) and origin, and survives reloads in that tab. A new tab starts empty; "Duplicate tab" starts with a copy, after which the two diverge. Use `localStorage` or the server for data that should follow the user.
questions.asked: Choosing session versus local storage for form drafts is a common design question.

questions.q: A draft autosave writes to `localStorage` on every keystroke. In production it sometimes throws. What is the most likely error, and the right handling?
choices: `QuotaExceededError` when the origin's few-MB quota is full; catch it and degrade
`SecurityError` when the page is served over plain HTTP; switch to cookies
`TypeError` when the value is longer than 64 KB; split it into chunks
`InvalidStateError` when another tab writes the same key; retry after a delay
questions.why: Each origin gets roughly 5 MB for localStorage, and `setItem` throws a `QuotaExceededError` when that is full; some privacy modes and blocked-storage settings throw on access too. Wrap reads and writes in try/catch and keep the app working without storage. There is no per-value 64 KB limit and concurrent writes from tabs do not throw.
questions.asked: It shows whether you treat browser storage as unreliable, which is what production code has to do.

questions.q: Why is `localStorage` a poor fit for caching a few thousand API records in an offline-capable app?
choices: It is cleared automatically whenever the user closes the browser
It is synchronous, string-only and small, so large reads block the main thread
It is only readable from a service worker, not from page scripts
It is shared between origins, so the data could leak to other sites
questions.why: Every `getItem` and `setItem` blocks the main thread, everything must be serialised to strings, and the quota is only a few megabytes. IndexedDB is asynchronous, stores structured data including Blobs, supports indexes and has far larger quotas. localStorage survives restarts, is per origin, and is not available in service workers at all.
questions.asked: The follow-up is usually "so what would you use?", and IndexedDB via a small wrapper is the expected answer.

questions.q: Inside an IndexedDB transaction, the code awaits a `fetch` before writing the result. The write fails with `TransactionInactiveError`. Why?
choices: IndexedDB forbids network calls from inside a page's event loop
`put` needs the key passed separately when the store has a keyPath
A readwrite transaction times out after one second of any activity
The transaction auto-commits once no request is pending at a task boundary
questions.why: IndexedDB transactions stay alive only while requests are queued; when control returns to the event loop with nothing pending, they commit. Waiting on a network request lets that happen, so the later `put` hits a finished transaction. Fetch first, then open the transaction and do all the IndexedDB work without awaiting anything else.
questions.asked: This is the classic IndexedDB trap, and it shows you have used the API rather than only named it.

questions.q: What does the Cache API (`caches.open(...)`) store, and how does it differ from the browser's HTTP cache?
choices: The same entries as the HTTP cache, exposed read-only to scripts
Arbitrary JSON values keyed by string, like localStorage but larger
Request/Response pairs you add and remove yourself; it ignores cache headers
Compiled JavaScript modules, so the browser can skip parsing them
questions.why: The Cache API is a programmable store of Request/Response pairs, normally used by a service worker to serve assets or API responses offline. Entries stay until your code deletes them or the browser evicts the origin; `Cache-Control` does not expire them. The HTTP cache is separate and driven entirely by headers.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know the layers of caching a PWA juggles and who controls each.

questions.q: Your chat widget runs in an iframe from `widget.example` on many customer sites. In current Chrome, Firefox and Safari, what does its `localStorage` look like?
choices: One store for `widget.example`, shared across every embedding site
A separate store per top-level site, since third-party storage is partitioned
No storage at all: cross-origin iframes may not use localStorage
The embedding site's own store, since the iframe inherits its origin
questions.why: Browsers now partition storage for third-party contexts by the top-level site, so the widget on shop-a.com and on shop-b.com sees two separate stores and cannot track users across them. First-party visits to `widget.example` get yet another store. The iframe keeps its own origin; it does not borrow the host page's.
questions.asked: Embedded widgets and SSO iframes break on this, so it signals current platform knowledge.

questions.q: What does this line do to the existing cookies for the page?
questions.code: document.cookie = 'theme=dark; path=/; max-age=31536000';
choices: Replaces the whole cookie string with just `theme=dark`
Throws unless the page removes every cookie first
Adds `theme` to a copy that is sent only once the page reloads
Sets or updates just the `theme` cookie and leaves the others alone
questions.why: `document.cookie` is an accessor: assigning sets one cookie, with its attributes, and reading returns all script-visible cookies as `name=value; name2=value2`. Cookies marked `HttpOnly` never appear when reading and cannot be written from script. The new cookie is sent on the very next request.
questions.asked: The odd getter/setter API is a common quiz item, and a good lead-in to HttpOnly.

questions.q: A logout handler tries to delete a cookie that was set with `path=/app`. Why does the cookie survive?
questions.code: document.cookie = 'prefs=; max-age=0';
choices: `max-age=0` is invalid, so the browser ignores the whole assignment
Deleting needs the same path (and domain) as the cookie was set with
Cookies can only be deleted by the server with a `Set-Cookie` header
The empty value is kept as a valid cookie until the session ends
questions.why: Cookies are identified by name, domain and path, so an expiring cookie with the default path (the current directory) is a different cookie and the `/app` one remains. Repeat the original `path` and `domain` with `max-age=0`. Script can delete any non-HttpOnly cookie it could have set.
questions.asked: "Logout does not log me out" is a real bug report, and this is often why.

questions.q: A cookie is set by `app.example.com` with no `Domain` attribute. Which requests carry it?
choices: Only requests to `app.example.com` itself
Requests to `example.com` and every one of its subdomains
Requests to `app.example.com` and to any of its own subdomains
Requests to any host, provided the scheme and port match
questions.why: Without `Domain`, a cookie is host-only: sent back to the exact host that set it. Setting `Domain=example.com` widens it to `example.com` and every subdomain, which is how shared login across `app.` and `admin.` works and why you should not widen it casually. A host cannot set a cookie for an unrelated domain.
questions.asked: Cookie scoping comes up whenever an app spans subdomains, and the host-only default surprises people.

questions.q: A cookie is set with `Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly; Secure`. When does the browser discard it?
choices: After 24 hours, the default lifetime for cookies without an expiry
When the tab that received it closes
When the browser session ends, as it has no `Expires` or `Max-Age`
Never, until the server sends a replacement with the same name
questions.why: A cookie with no `Expires` or `Max-Age` is a session cookie, dropped when the browser session ends. Browsers that restore sessions on start-up may keep them, so do not rely on it for security; give auth cookies an explicit lifetime and expire sessions server-side. It is not per tab.
questions.asked: A basic cookie-lifetime check that often leads into how "remember me" is implemented.

questions.q: Your SPA on `https://app.example.com` calls `https://api.example.com` with plain `fetch(url)`. The API relies on a session cookie. What happens?
choices: The cookie is sent, since both hosts share the `example.com` domain
The cookie is sent only on GET requests, not on POST
Not sent: cross-origin fetch omits credentials by default
The request is blocked before sending, since cookies need a preflight
questions.why: `fetch` defaults to `credentials: 'same-origin'`, and a different subdomain is a different origin. Pass `credentials: 'include'`, and the API must answer with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and a specific `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. The same-site relationship affects `SameSite`, not this default.
questions.asked: "Login works in Postman but not in the app" is a daily question, and this is half the answer.

questions.q: The fetch uses `credentials: 'include'`, and the API answers with these headers. What does the browser do?
questions.code:
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
choices: Allows it: the wildcard covers every origin, including this one
Blocks the response: credentialed requests need an exact origin
Allows it, but strips the cookies from the next request
Allows it only if the request method is GET or HEAD
questions.why: For credentialed requests the wildcard is not allowed: the server must echo the specific origin (and add `Vary: Origin` so caches keep them apart). Otherwise the browser hides the response from your script, even though the server has already processed the request.
questions.asked: The wildcard-plus-credentials failure is the most common CORS mistake in real APIs.

questions.q: To "fix" a CORS error, someone adds `mode: 'no-cors'`. What does the code now get back?
questions.code:
const res = await fetch('https://api.other.com/data', { mode: 'no-cors' });
console.log(res.type, res.status);
choices: `cors 200`, with the JSON body readable as normal
`basic 200`, since the request is now treated as same-origin
`opaque 0`, with no readable headers or body
Nothing: the fetch rejects with a TypeError before sending
questions.why: `no-cors` sends a simple request and gives you an opaque response: status 0, no headers and an empty body, so there is no data to use. It exists for cases like caching a cross-origin image in a service worker. The fix for CORS is on the server, or a same-origin proxy.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to check that you know CORS is solved server-side, not by a client flag.

questions.q: The API sends `X-Total-Count: 240` on a cross-origin response, and DevTools shows it. Why does `res.headers.get('X-Total-Count')` return `null`?
choices: Header names must be lower-cased when read through the Headers object
Custom headers are only readable after the body has been consumed
Headers starting with `X-` are reserved and always hidden from script
The server did not name it in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`
questions.why: On a CORS response, script can read only the safelisted headers such as `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control`; anything else must be named in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`. DevTools shows the raw network response, which is why it looks present. `Headers.get` is case-insensitive.
questions.asked: Pagination via headers trips on this, and it proves you have debugged CORS past the preflight.

questions.q: A cross-origin request fails CORS. What can your JavaScript learn about the failure?
choices: Only that `fetch` rejected with a `TypeError`; details are in the console
The HTTP status code, via the `status` field on the rejection error
The name of the missing header, from `error.message`
Nothing: the promise stays pending until the page is reloaded
questions.why: A CORS failure is deliberately indistinguishable from a network error in script: `fetch` rejects with a `TypeError`, so a page cannot probe other origins. The browser console and Network panel show the real reason. The server may still have run the request, which matters for non-idempotent calls.
questions.asked: It tests your debugging path: go to the console and Network panel, not the error object.

questions.q: Which URL is the same origin as `https://app.example.com/dashboard`?
choices: `https://app.example.com:443/settings`
`http://app.example.com/dashboard`
`https://api.example.com/dashboard`
`https://app.example.com:8443/dashboard`
questions.why: An origin is scheme, host and port, and 443 is the default port for https, so the first URL has the same origin despite the explicit port. Changing the scheme, the subdomain or the port makes a different origin. Paths never matter.
questions.asked: Every CORS and cookie question rests on this definition, so it often opens the topic.

questions.q: In development the React app runs on `localhost:5173` and the API on `localhost:3000`, and calls hit CORS errors. Why does a Vite `server.proxy` for `/api` make them go away?
choices: The proxy adds `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` to every API response
The browser calls the dev server on its own origin, which forwards server-side
Vite turns off the browser's CORS checks for localhost while it is running
Proxied requests are sent with `mode: 'no-cors'` and patched on return
questions.why: With a proxy the page fetches `/api/...` from `localhost:5173`, which is same-origin, and the dev server makes the call to port 3000 itself; CORS does not apply between servers. Different ports are different origins, which is why the direct call failed. Production then needs the same shape (a reverse proxy) or real CORS headers.
questions.asked: Knowing why the dev proxy works stops people assuming the same code will work unchanged in production.

questions.q: What happens here?
choices: `raw` is an empty string, since the body was already consumed
`raw` holds the JSON text, since the body is cached after the first read
The third line rejects with a TypeError: a body can be read only once
`items` is undefined, because `text()` replaces the parsed result
questions.why: A response body is a stream, and reading it once marks it used, so the second read rejects ("body has already been read"). Read it once as text and `JSON.parse` it yourself, or `res.clone()` before the first read if two consumers need it.
questions.asked: Logging a failed response body is where most people meet this, so it tests real debugging.

questions.q: A DELETE endpoint answers `204 No Content`. What does this code do?
choices: Resolves to `null`, the JSON value of an empty body
Resolves to `{}`, since 204 is treated as an empty object
Resolves to `undefined`, because there is no content type
Rejects with a SyntaxError, as an empty body is not valid JSON
questions.why: `res.json()` parses the body text, and an empty string is not JSON, so it rejects with `SyntaxError: Unexpected end of JSON input`. Check `res.status === 204` (or the content length or type) before parsing; a generic API client should handle it once, centrally.
questions.asked: A generic fetch wrapper has to handle this, so it is a quick check of API-client experience.

questions.q: An Express API with `express.json()` receives `req.body` as `{}` from this call. Why?
choices: Express reads bodies only on PUT and PATCH requests, not on POST
`JSON.stringify` escapes quotes, so the server cannot parse the result
A string body is sent as `text/plain`, which the JSON parser skips
The body is not sent, since fetch drops string bodies without `Content-Length`
questions.why: Given a string body, fetch sets `Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8`, and `express.json()` only parses requests whose type is JSON. Add `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }`. That header also makes the request non-simple, so cross-origin calls get a preflight.
questions.asked: Probably the most common first bug when wiring a frontend to an API.

questions.q: An upload sends a `FormData` with a file. The server fails to parse it after someone added this header. Why?
choices: Multipart uploads must be sent with PUT, never with POST
The header lacks the boundary the browser would have generated
FormData must be converted to a Blob before it can be sent
The header must be `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` for files
questions.why: Multipart bodies are split by a random boundary that must appear in the header (`multipart/form-data; boundary=…`). When you pass a `FormData` body and no content type, fetch sets it correctly; setting it by hand overrides that with a header the server cannot use. Leave it out.
questions.asked: File-upload bugs are common in CRUD apps, and this one is easy to spot once you know it.

questions.q: What does this throw or send?
choices: It sends the JSON as the body of a GET request
It moves the body into the query string automatically
It sends the GET, silently dropping the body
It throws a TypeError: GET and HEAD cannot have a body
questions.why: The Fetch standard forbids a body on GET and HEAD, so building the request throws a `TypeError` before anything is sent. Put search parameters in the query string with `URLSearchParams`, or use POST for a complex search.
questions.asked: It checks you know where GET parameters go and that fetch enforces it.

questions.q: Which code builds the query string for a search of `rock & roll` on page 2?
choices: Interpolate `q` straight into `/api/songs?q=…&page=2`
Wrap `q` in `encodeURI()` before interpolating it
Build it with `new URLSearchParams({ q, page: 2 })`
Wrap `q` in `escape()` before interpolating it
questions.why: `URLSearchParams` encodes each key and value, so `&` becomes `%26` and the space becomes `+`, giving `q=rock+%26+roll&page=2`. Raw interpolation and `encodeURI` leave `&` alone, so the server sees `q=rock ` and a stray ` roll` parameter; `escape` is deprecated and mishandles non-ASCII.
questions.asked: Search boxes that break on special characters are a standard bug, and this is the fix interviewers want.

questions.q: What does this log?
choices: `hello world tag=c&q=hello+world`
`hello+world tag=a&tag=b&tag=c&q=hello+world`
`hello world tag=a&tag=c&q=hello+world`
`hello+world tag=c&q=hello%20world`
questions.why: In the query-string format `+` means a space, so `get('q')` decodes it to "hello world". `set` replaces every existing value for the key with one, while `append` adds another; `getAll` reads repeated keys such as multi-select filters.
questions.asked: Filter UIs with multi-value parameters depend on knowing set versus append.

questions.q: The page is at `https://shop.example/app/orders`. Which URL does `fetch('api/orders')` request?
choices: `https://shop.example/api/orders`
`https://shop.example/app/orders/api/orders`
`https://shop.example/app/api/orders`
`https://api.shop.example/orders`
questions.why: A relative path without a leading slash resolves against the current URL's directory, and `orders` is the last segment, so it is replaced: `/app/api/orders`. With client-side routing the directory changes as the user navigates, so API paths should start with `/` or be built from a configured base URL.
questions.asked: Explains the "API calls 404 only on nested routes" bug in single-page apps.

questions.q: A streamed response is decoded chunk by chunk like this. What bug appears with non-English text?
choices: Characters split across chunks turn into replacement characters (�)
Every chunk after the first is decoded as Latin-1 instead of UTF-8
Nothing: `TextDecoder` always buffers incomplete characters itself
The loop never ends, because `done` is only set for text responses
questions.why: Network chunks split on byte boundaries, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character can arrive in two halves, and decoding each half alone yields �. Pass `{ stream: true }` so the decoder keeps partial bytes for the next call, or pipe through a `TextDecoderStream`.
questions.asked: Streaming AI or log output is common now, and this bug only shows with real-world text.

questions.q: A file upload screen needs a progress bar for the upload itself. What should it use in 2026?
choices: `fetch` with an `onprogress` callback passed in the init options
`XMLHttpRequest`, listening to `xhr.upload` progress events
The `Content-Length` response header read after the upload ends
A `ReadableStream` response body, read chunk by chunk as it downloads
questions.why: `fetch` has no upload-progress events; `XMLHttpRequest` still does, through `xhr.upload.onprogress`. Streaming request bodies with fetch need HTTP/2 and `duplex: 'half'` and are not supported everywhere, so XHR (or a library over it) remains the practical answer. Reading the response body tracks download progress, not upload.
questions.asked: A practical "why would you still use XHR" question with a clear right answer.

questions.q: A request is given `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000)` and the server takes 10 seconds. What does the `catch` see?
choices: A `DOMException` named `AbortError`, the same as a manual abort
A `TypeError` "Failed to fetch", the same as a network error
A `DOMException` named `TimeoutError`
Nothing: the promise resolves with a 408 response
questions.why: `AbortSignal.timeout()` aborts with a `TimeoutError` DOMException, so you can tell a timeout from a user cancel, which uses `AbortError`. Combine both with `AbortSignal.any([userSignal, AbortSignal.timeout(5000)])`. Nothing synthesises a 408.
questions.asked: Timeouts are a standard API-client requirement, and distinguishing them from cancels is the mid-level detail.

questions.q: A static host serves only `index.html` and cannot be configured with rewrites. Why does a hash router (`/#/orders/7`) work there when a path router (`/orders/7`) 404s on reload?
choices: The fragment is never sent to the server, which always receives `/`
Static hosts rewrite any URL with `#` in it back to `index.html`
Hash URLs are cached by the browser, so reloads never hit the server
Path routers need Node on the server to render each route first
questions.why: Everything after `#` stays in the browser, so a reload of `/#/orders/7` requests `/` and the app reads `location.hash`, listening for `hashchange`. A path router asks the server for `/orders/7`, which must be rewritten to `index.html` (the "SPA fallback") or it 404s.
questions.asked: It shows you understand what the server sees for client-side routes, the root of every "404 on refresh" ticket.

questions.q: After a successful login you send the user to the dashboard. Which call stops Back returning them to the login page?
choices: `location.href = '/dashboard'`
`location.assign('/dashboard')`
`history.pushState({}, '', '/dashboard')`
`location.replace('/dashboard')`
questions.why: `location.replace` navigates and replaces the current history entry, so the login page is no longer behind the dashboard. Setting `href` and `assign` both add an entry, and `pushState` adds one without even loading the page. Router libraries expose the same idea as a `replace` option.
questions.asked: A small UX detail that separates people who have built auth flows from those who have only read about them.

questions.q: An OAuth-style flow returns `https://app.example/callback#token=abc`. What does the server hosting `/callback` receive?
choices: The path `/callback` only; the fragment stays in the browser
The full URL including `#token=abc`, in the request line
The token, as a `Referer` header added by the browser
Nothing, since fragment URLs are served from the browser cache
questions.why: Browsers strip the fragment before sending a request, so only client-side script can read it, through `location.hash`. That is why the implicit flow used fragments, and also why it is discouraged: the token lives in browser history and script. Referer headers exclude fragments too.
questions.asked: It checks your model of what a URL sends, which matters for routing, analytics and auth.

questions.q: This script is in the `<head>`. Why does it throw "Cannot read properties of null"?
choices: External scripts cannot use `querySelector` until `load` has fired
The `id` must be quoted with single quotes to match the selector
The script runs as soon as it is parsed, before `#root` exists
`#root` is only created after the first paint of the page
questions.why: A classic script without `defer` or `async` blocks parsing and runs immediately, when the parser has not reached the body yet, so `querySelector` returns `null`. Add `defer`, use `type="module"`, or put the script at the end of the body.
questions.asked: A first-week bug; the strong answer names `defer` rather than wrapping everything in an event listener.

questions.q: You move a CSV export into a Web Worker. Which line fails inside the worker?
choices:
`const csv = rows.map(toLine).join('
');`
`postMessage(new Blob([csv], { type: 'text/csv' }));`
`const res = await fetch('/api/rows'); const rows = await res.json();`
`document.querySelector('#status').textContent = 'Done';`
questions.why: Workers run on their own thread with no access to the DOM, `window` or `document`, so they post results back and the page updates the UI. They do have `fetch`, timers, `Blob`, IndexedDB and `postMessage`, which is what makes them useful for heavy data work.
questions.asked: It checks you know what a worker can and cannot do before proposing one to fix a janky page.

questions.q: A dashboard polls an API every 10 seconds. Which event lets it stop polling while the tab is in the background?
choices: `blur` on `window`, which fires whenever the tab is hidden
`pagehide`, which fires when the user switches to another tab
`visibilitychange`, reading `document.visibilityState`
`freeze`, which fires as soon as the tab loses focus
questions.why: The Page Visibility API fires `visibilitychange` when the tab is hidden or shown, and `document.visibilityState` says which. `blur` also fires when focus moves to devtools or an iframe while the tab is visible, and `pagehide` is about navigating away. Libraries such as TanStack Query use this to refetch on return.
questions.asked: Saving server load and battery on background tabs is a practical concern, and this is the standard tool.

questions.q: An `<input type="number">` holds 5. What is `input.value + 1`?
choices: `NaN`
It throws, since number inputs have no string value
questions.why: Every input's `value` is a string, whatever its type, so this concatenates. Use `input.valueAsNumber`, which is `NaN` when the field is empty or invalid, or `Number(input.value)`. Date inputs likewise offer `valueAsDate`.
questions.asked: A quick check that you do not trust input types to give you typed values.

questions.q: A filter form has three checkboxes named `status`, and two are ticked. What does this return?
questions.code:
const data = new FormData(form);
data.getAll('status');
choices: An array of the two ticked checkboxes' values
The value of the last ticked checkbox as a string
An array of three values, with `null` for the unticked one
The string `"on,on"`, joined in document order
questions.why: FormData keeps repeated names as separate entries, and unticked checkboxes are not included at all, so `getAll` returns the two ticked values. `get` returns only the first. A checkbox with no `value` attribute submits `"on"`.
questions.asked: Multi-select filters are everywhere in CRUD apps, and this is how you read them without a framework.

questions.q: Why does this throw?
questions.code:
class UserCard extends HTMLElement {}
customElements.define('usercard', UserCard);
