choices: Custom element names must contain a hyphen, such as `user-card`
The class needs a `constructor` that calls `super()` first
Custom elements must be defined before the document has loaded
Names must match the class name exactly, as `UserCard`
questions.why: Valid custom element names are lower-case and contain a hyphen, which keeps them apart from current and future built-in elements. An implicit constructor already calls `super()`, and elements can be defined at any time; existing tags in the page are upgraded when the definition arrives.
questions.asked: The entry-level web-components check; the hyphen rule is the thing everyone forgets once.

questions.q: A "Copy link" button calls `navigator.clipboard.writeText(url)`. It works locally but `navigator.clipboard` is `undefined` on the staging server. What is the likely cause?
choices: Staging serves over plain HTTP, and the API needs a secure context
The call is missing `await`, so it has not finished yet
The button needs a `type="button"` attribute to allow copying
Staging has no Permissions-Policy header, which the API requires
questions.why: The async Clipboard API exists only in secure contexts: HTTPS, or `localhost`, which is why it worked locally. Writing also needs a recent user gesture in most browsers. Missing `await` would not make the property undefined.
questions.asked: It checks you know about secure contexts, which gate a growing list of browser APIs.

questions.q: Which page counts as a secure context, so that APIs like `crypto.randomUUID()` and service workers are available?
choices: `http://192.168.1.20:3000`, a machine on the local network
`http://localhost:5173`, a dev server on your own machine
`http://staging.example.com`, behind a company VPN
`file:///C:/app/index.html`, opened from disk
questions.why: Secure contexts are HTTPS pages plus loopback addresses (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`), which browsers trust for development. A LAN IP or internal hostname over HTTP is not secure, however private the network, which is why testing on a phone via your laptop's IP can lose these APIs.
questions.asked: The phone-testing gotcha is common, and knowing the localhost exception explains it.

questions.q: An "Export CSV" button builds the file in the browser. Which code downloads it with a proper filename?
choices: `window.open('data:text/csv,' + csv)` in a new tab
`location.href = csv` with a `Content-Disposition` meta tag
A `Blob`, an object URL and a clicked `<a download="orders.csv">`
`navigator.sendBeacon('/download', csv)` to trigger a save
questions.why: Wrap the text in a `Blob`, create a URL with `URL.createObjectURL`, point a temporary `<a download>` at it and click it, then revoke the URL. `download` is honoured for same-origin and blob URLs. Popups of data URLs are blocked or open in a tab, and `sendBeacon` is fire-and-forget to a server.
questions.asked: Client-side exports are a common CRUD feature, and the Blob-URL pattern is the expected answer.

questions.q: An avatar picker should preview the chosen image before upload. Which is the lightest correct approach?
choices: Upload the file first and show the URL the server returns
Read `input.value`, which is the file's path, and set it as `src`
Set `img.src = URL.createObjectURL(file)` and revoke the old URL
Call `JSON.stringify(file)` and set the result as a data URL
questions.why: An object URL points straight at the File in memory, so the preview is instant and no copy is made; call `URL.revokeObjectURL` when it is replaced to free it. `input.value` is a fake path such as `C:\fakepath\me.png` for privacy, and a File does not serialise to JSON.
questions.asked: A common upload-form feature that checks you know the File and Blob APIs.

questions.q: An `<input type="file" multiple>` has three files chosen. Why does `input.files.map(upload)` throw?
choices: `files` is `null` until the form has been submitted
`files` is a FileList, which is array-like but has no `map`
`files` holds file paths, and `upload` expects File objects
`multiple` inputs expose files through `input.value` instead
questions.why: `input.files` is a `FileList`, indexable and iterable but not an Array, so it lacks `map`. Convert with `Array.from(input.files)` or spread it. `NodeList` and `HTMLCollection` have the same shape and the same trap.
questions.asked: Array-likes in the DOM trip up people who learned JavaScript through arrays only.

questions.q: An offline banner uses `navigator.onLine`. Users on a captive hotel Wi-Fi portal see "Online" but every request fails. Why?
choices: `onLine` is only updated when the page is reloaded
`onLine` only reports whether the device has a network connection
`onLine` is always true on HTTPS pages, for privacy reasons
`onLine` checks the server of the current page, which is cached
questions.why: `navigator.onLine` and the `online`/`offline` events reflect whether a network interface is up, not whether the internet or your API is reachable. Treat `false` as a reliable offline signal, but for "online" check failed requests or ping your own health endpoint.
questions.asked: Offline-aware UIs are a common feature request, and this is where naive versions fail.

questions.q: You log `order` in the console, then mutate it on the next line. When you expand the logged object in DevTools, what do you see?
questions.code:
console.log(order);
order.status = 'paid';
choices: The status as it was when logged, since logs are snapshots
An error, because the object changed after it was logged
`[object Object]`, since objects are logged as strings
The status as it is now, since expanding reads the live object
questions.why: Chrome and Firefox log a reference; the preview line may show the old value, but expanding reads the object as it is at that moment, so you see `paid`. For a snapshot, log `structuredClone(order)` or `JSON.stringify(order)`, or use a breakpoint.
questions.asked: A classic debugging trap; knowing it saves hours of chasing a mutation that did not happen when you thought.

questions.q: You append an existing `<li>` to a second list. What happens to the first list?
questions.code:
const item = listA.querySelector('li');
listB.append(item);
choices: Nothing: the `<li>` now appears in both lists
The `<li>` moves: a node can only be in one place
It throws, since the item must be removed first
listA keeps a placeholder until the next render
questions.why: Appending a node that is already in the document moves it, keeping its listeners and state. To have it in both places, append `item.cloneNode(true)`, remembering clones lose `addEventListener` listeners. Drag-to-reorder lists rely on this move behaviour.
questions.asked: The basis of reorderable lists and kanban boards, so it is a common framework-free question.

questions.q: What does `btn.closest('button')` return when `btn` is itself a `<button>`?
choices: `btn` itself
Its nearest button ancestor, or `null`
`null`, as only ancestors are checked
The first button in the document
questions.why: `closest` tests the element itself first, then walks up its ancestors, returning the first match or `null`. That is exactly why `e.target.closest('button')` works whether the click landed on the button or on an icon inside it.
questions.asked: A quick check that underpins every delegation answer.

questions.q: In a hand-rolled router, a click listener on `<a href="/orders">` calls `history.pushState` and renders. What must it do to stop the browser also loading `/orders`?
choices: Call `e.stopPropagation()` so the click never reaches the document
Return `false` from a listener added with `addEventListener`
Remove the `href`, since links with one always navigate
Call `e.preventDefault()` to cancel the link's default navigation
questions.why: `preventDefault` cancels the default action, here following the link, while the element keeps its `href` for accessibility, middle-click and copy-link. `stopPropagation` affects other listeners, not the default, and `return false` only cancels in `on…` properties and jQuery.
questions.asked: The core of every client-side router, and a clean check on default actions versus propagation.

questions.q: What does this line do when the page has no element with class `.toast`?
questions.code: document.querySelector('.toast').remove();
choices: Nothing: `remove()` on no match is a silent no-op
Throws a TypeError, since `querySelector` returned `null`
Removes the `<body>`, which is the default match
Throws a SyntaxError, since `.toast` is not a valid selector
questions.why: `querySelector` returns `null` when nothing matches, and calling a method on `null` throws. Use optional chaining (`?.remove()`) when absence is expected, and let it throw when absence is a bug. `querySelectorAll` returns an empty NodeList instead.
questions.asked: The most common DOM error message, so it is a quick screen for everyday experience.

questions.q: A settings page should follow the OS dark-mode setting live, even if the user changes it while the page is open. Which code does that?
choices: Read `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches` once on load
Listen for `change` on `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)')`
Listen for `resize` on `window` and re-check the colour scheme
Poll `screen.colorDepth` every second and compare it with before
questions.why: `matchMedia` returns a MediaQueryList whose `matches` gives the current answer and whose `change` event fires when it flips. Reading once misses later changes, and the OS theme has nothing to do with resizing or colour depth. In pure CSS the `prefers-color-scheme` media query already updates live.
questions.asked: Theming is a common feature, and it shows you can use media queries from JavaScript.

questions.q: After saving, a long form should bring its success banner into view smoothly. Which call does that?
choices: `banner.focus({ behavior: 'smooth', preventScroll: false })`
`window.scrollTo(banner, { behavior: 'smooth' })`
`banner.scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth' })`
`document.body.scrollTop = banner.offsetTop`
questions.why: `scrollIntoView` scrolls every scrollable ancestor as needed to show the element, with options for smooth motion and alignment. `scrollTo` takes coordinates, not an element, and `offsetTop` is only document-relative when no ancestor is positioned. A sticky header can be allowed for with CSS `scroll-margin-top`.
questions.asked: A small everyday API; the `scroll-margin-top` follow-up is a nice extra.

questions.q: A page reads `?tab=billing` from its URL. Which line is correct?
choices: `new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('tab')`
`location.searchParams.get('tab')`
`location.query.get('tab')`
`new URL(location.search).searchParams.get('tab')`
questions.why: `location.search` is the raw string `?tab=billing`, and `URLSearchParams` parses it, handling the leading `?` and decoding. `location` has no `searchParams` or `query` of its own (URL objects do), and `new URL('?tab=billing')` throws because it is not an absolute URL; `new URL(location.href).searchParams.get('tab')` would work.
questions.asked: Reading state from the URL is basic router work, and a good habit for shareable filters.

questions.q: In a classic `<script>` (not a module), a colleague defines `const config = {...}` at the top level. Where is it visible?
choices: Only inside that script file, like a module-scoped variable
To every classic script on the page, but not as `window.config`
As `window.config`, like a top-level `var` would be
Nowhere after the script ends, since it is garbage collected
questions.why: Top-level `let`, `const` and `class` in classic scripts go into a shared global scope visible to every classic script, but unlike `var` and function declarations they do not become `window` properties. Module scripts keep their top-level bindings private, which is one reason to use them.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand global scope in the browser and why modules replaced it.

questions.q: A drop zone logs from its `drop` handler, but dropping files on it just opens them in the browser. Why?
choices: `dataTransfer` is only readable in `dragstart`, not in `drop`
Drop zones need the `draggable="true"` attribute to accept files
Files can only be dropped onto an `<input type="file">`
`dragover` must also call `preventDefault`, or `drop` never fires
questions.why: By default elements are not drop targets; cancelling `dragover` (and usually `dragenter`) is how an element says it accepts the drop. Without it the drop goes to the browser's default, opening the file. `draggable` is for drag sources, and `dataTransfer.files` is readable in `drop`.
questions.asked: Drag-and-drop upload is a common feature, and the `dragover` rule is the one thing people forget.

questions.q: A form has two submit buttons, `<button name="action" value="draft">` and `value="publish"`. In the submit handler, how do you know which was clicked?
choices: `e.target`, which is the button that was pressed
`document.activeElement`, which is always the pressed button
`new FormData(form).get('action')`, which includes it
`e.submitter`, the button or input that triggered submission
questions.why: `SubmitEvent.submitter` is the button that submitted the form (or `null` for `requestSubmit()` without one). `e.target` is the form, `activeElement` is unreliable because Safari does not focus buttons on click, and `new FormData(form)` omits the submitter unless you pass it as the second argument.
questions.asked: Save-draft versus publish is a common requirement, and `submitter` is the clean answer.

questions.q: A router intercepts every click on internal links and calls `pushState`. Users complain that Ctrl+click no longer opens a new tab. What should the handler check before intercepting?
choices: Whether the link is inside `<nav>`, since only nav links should route
Whether `e.isTrusted` is true, since modified clicks are synthetic
Modifier keys, the mouse button, `target`, `download` and origin
Whether the `href` ends in `.html`, which marks a full navigation
questions.why: A good link interceptor bails out on `e.button !== 0`, Ctrl/Meta/Shift/Alt, `target="_blank"`, a `download` attribute or a cross-origin `href`, and on `e.defaultPrevented`. Everything else can be routed client-side. Router libraries' `<Link>` components do exactly these checks.
questions.asked: It separates people who have used a router from people who have thought about what one must preserve.

questions.q: Your app embeds a payment iframe and listens for its result. What is missing?
choices: A check that `e.origin` is the payment provider's origin
A call to `e.preventDefault()` so the iframe stops retrying
`{ passive: true }`, since message handlers must not block
A `JSON.parse(e.data)`, since messages are always strings
questions.why: Any window that can get a reference to yours, including a page that opened it, can post messages, so accept only those whose `origin` matches the expected sender. Likewise, give `postMessage` an explicit target origin rather than `'*'` when sending secrets. Messages are structured-cloned, not only strings.
questions.asked: A standard security review item for widgets, OAuth popups and payment frames.

questions.q: An error reporter hooks `window.onerror`. Which failures does it miss?
choices: Errors thrown inside `setTimeout` callbacks
Promise rejections that nothing handles
Errors thrown by inline `onclick` attributes
Errors from scripts added dynamically after load
questions.why: Uncaught exceptions go to the `error` event, but a rejected promise with no handler fires a separate `unhandledrejection` event on `window`, and with async code everywhere that is most failures. Register both. Timer callbacks, inline handlers and later-loaded scripts all reach `onerror`.
questions.asked: It shows you know how production error tracking works in the browser, not just in try/catch.

questions.q: Two scripts in the head: `analytics.js` then `widget.js`, both with `async`. `widget.js` depends on `analytics.js`. What goes wrong, and what fixes it?
choices: Nothing: `async` scripts run in document order once both are loaded
They can run in either order; `defer` keeps order and waits for parsing
They run before parsing ends; `type="module"` alone keeps them ordered
The second one never runs; `async` allows one script per document
questions.why: `async` scripts run as soon as each one arrives, so a smaller or cached `widget.js` can run first. `defer` scripts download in parallel but run in document order after parsing, so dependent scripts should use `defer` (module scripts behave like `defer` unless marked `async`).
questions.asked: The async-versus-defer ordering follow-up is what interviewers use after "what does defer do".

questions.q: A username field shows "Name taken" via a custom validity message. After the user picks a free name, the form still refuses to submit. Why?
questions.code:
const res = await checkName(input.value);
if (res.taken) input.setCustomValidity('Name taken');
choices: Custom validity is only re-checked after the page reloads
Nothing clears it: it stays invalid until `setCustomValidity('')`
`setCustomValidity` also adds `required`, which is still unmet
The async check needs `reportValidity()` before it can take effect
questions.why: A non-empty custom message makes the field invalid until you set it back to an empty string. Always set it on both branches, for example `input.setCustomValidity(res.taken ? 'Name taken' : '')`. It does not touch `required` and needs no reload.
questions.asked: The Constraint Validation API is how you add server-backed checks to native validation, and this is its main trap.

questions.q: What is the difference between `form.checkValidity()` and `form.reportValidity()`?
choices: `checkValidity` checks required fields only; `reportValidity` checks every constraint
`checkValidity` returns a boolean silently; `reportValidity` also shows the messages
`checkValidity` runs before submit; `reportValidity` only after a server response
`checkValidity` validates one field; `reportValidity` validates the whole form
questions.why: Both run every constraint and fire `invalid` on failing controls; `reportValidity` additionally shows the browser's messages and focuses the first invalid field. Both exist on forms and on individual controls. Use `checkValidity` to enable a button, `reportValidity` when the user tries to proceed.
questions.asked: Multi-step forms validate each step by hand, and this pair is how.

questions.q: A multi-select filter form is serialised like this. The user ticked the `open` and `overdue` statuses. What is sent?
questions.code:
const params = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
await fetch('/api/orders?' + new URLSearchParams(params));
choices: `status=open&status=overdue`
`status=open%2Coverdue`
`status=overdue`
`status=open`
questions.why: `Object.fromEntries` keeps one value per key, and the later entry overwrites the earlier one, so only `overdue` survives. Pass the FormData straight to `new URLSearchParams(formData)` to keep repeated keys, or collect them with `getAll`.
questions.asked: A subtle data-loss bug in a very common one-liner, which interviewers enjoy.

questions.q: A custom element starts a timer in `connectedCallback`. A drag-to-reorder list moves the element, and two timers are now running. Why?
choices: The constructor runs again on every move, re-creating the timer
`connectedCallback` runs on every insertion, so a move re-runs it
Moving an element clones it, and the clone gets its own timer
`attributeChangedCallback` fires on moves and calls connect again
questions.why: A move is a removal and an insertion, so `disconnectedCallback` then `connectedCallback` run again. Start work in connect and stop it in disconnect so the pair stays balanced. The constructor runs once per element.
questions.asked: Lifecycle symmetry is the core of web components, like effect cleanup in React.

questions.q: A `<user-badge>` element implements `attributeChangedCallback`, but changing its `name` attribute never calls it. What is missing?
choices: A `MutationObserver` registered in the constructor
A static `observedAttributes` getter that returns `['name']`
A `name` property setter that dispatches a change event
The `is="user-badge"` attribute on the element in the page
questions.why: For performance the browser only reports attributes listed in the class's static `observedAttributes`. List `name` there and the callback receives the name, old value and new value. Reflecting a property to the attribute is a separate, optional step.
questions.asked: Every web-components walkthrough hits this, so it is the standard follow-up to the lifecycle question.

questions.q: A product list updates `?sort=` as the user changes a dropdown. Why prefer `replaceState` over `pushState` here?
choices: `pushState` reloads the page, while `replaceState` does not
Back should leave the page, not step through every sort choice
`replaceState` fires `popstate`, so the list re-renders itself
`pushState` cannot change only the query string of a URL
questions.why: Each `pushState` adds a history entry, so rapid filter tweaks would make Back walk through every one. `replaceState` updates the URL, keeping it shareable, without growing history. Neither reloads or fires `popstate`; push is right for changes users think of as navigation.
questions.asked: It shows product thinking about URL state, not just knowing the two methods exist.

questions.q: A worker sends a 50 MB `ArrayBuffer` back to the page with `postMessage(buffer)`. Why is it slow, and what fixes it?
choices: It is structured-cloned; pass `[buffer]` as the transfer list to move it
It is JSON-encoded; wrap it in a `Blob` so it is sent as binary
It is sent over the network; use `SharedWorker` to keep it local
It is compressed; set `{ compress: false }` in the message options
questions.why: `postMessage` copies data with the structured clone algorithm, so 50 MB is duplicated. Listing the buffer in the transfer argument (`postMessage(buffer, [buffer])`) moves ownership instead, leaving the sender's buffer detached with length 0. Nothing is JSON-encoded, sent over a network or compressed.
questions.asked: Transferables are what make workers useful for heavy data, and knowing about detaching shows real use.

questions.q: A countdown in a background tab updates with `setInterval(tick, 100)`. When the user returns after a few minutes, the displayed time is well behind. Why?
choices: Intervals under 1 second are rounded up to 1 second on every page
Browsers throttle timers in hidden tabs, so far fewer ticks run
The interval stops for good once the tab is hidden, until reload
Hidden tabs run timers on a worker thread with a slower clock
questions.why: Browsers throttle timers in background tabs to at most about once a second, and Chrome throttles long-hidden pages to once a minute, so a counter that adds 100 ms per tick falls behind. Compute remaining time from `Date.now()` or `performance.now()` on each tick instead of counting ticks.
questions.asked: Timers, countdowns and session-expiry warnings all hit this, and the fix is a transferable habit.

questions.q: Your error tracker receives only `"Script error."` with no stack for errors in a script served from your CDN. What fixes it?
choices: Serve source maps next to the minified script on the CDN
Wrap the whole bundle in a top-level try/catch block
Add `crossorigin` to the tag and CORS headers on the CDN
Load the script with `type="module"` instead of classic
questions.why: Browsers hide error details from cross-origin scripts loaded without CORS, to stop pages learning about other origins. `crossorigin="anonymous"` plus `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on the CDN response unlocks the message and stack. Source maps only help once you have a stack; module scripts are fetched with CORS anyway but must then still get the header.
questions.asked: An obscure-looking message with a precise fix, which shows real production debugging experience.

questions.q: A form wants to log every field that fails validation when the user submits. Why does this listener never fire?
choices: `invalid` fires on the form only after `submit` has been cancelled
`invalid` fires only when `reportValidity()` is called explicitly
It fires on each control and does not bubble; use capture
`invalid` is suppressed when the form has the `novalidate` attribute
questions.why: The `invalid` event is dispatched at each failing control with `bubbles: false`, so a form listener only hears it with `{ capture: true }`. It fires during interactive submission and from `checkValidity`/`reportValidity`. `novalidate` would stop validation, but nothing here sets it.
questions.asked: Custom error summaries are built on this event, and the capture trick is the detail that proves you built one.

questions.q: A "Publish" button submits a form handled with fetch. Why does the server never receive `action=publish`?
questions.code:
<button name="action" value="publish">Publish</button>
<script>
form.addEventListener('submit', (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  fetch('/posts', { method: 'POST', body: new FormData(form) });
});
</script>
choices: `FormData` skips `<button>` elements unless they have a `type="submit"`
`new FormData(form)` omits the submitter; pass `e.submitter` as its second argument
The server must read button values from the query string, not the body
Named buttons are sent only when the form has a `method="post"` attribute
questions.why: A native submission includes the clicked button's name and value, but constructing FormData from the form alone has no idea which button was used. `new FormData(form, e.submitter)` adds it in document order, matching native behaviour. Buttons default to `type="submit"` already.
questions.asked: Progressive-enhancement forms depend on parity with native submission, and this is the gap people miss.

questions.q: A custom element dispatches `bubbles: true` events from inside its shadow root. Page code listening on `document` never sees them. What is missing?
choices: `composed: true`, so the event crosses the shadow boundary
`cancelable: true`, which is required for events that carry a `detail`
A `slot` element, since events only leave through slots
`mode: 'open'` on `attachShadow`, which closed roots lack
questions.why: Without `composed: true`, an event stops at the shadow root. With it, the event continues into the light DOM, retargeted so outside listeners see the host element as `target`. Open versus closed shadow roots do not change event propagation.
questions.asked: The composed flag is the key idea behind component events in shadow DOM, and few people know it.

questions.q: What does this server-rendered markup give you without any JavaScript running?
questions.code: Ada Lovelace
choices: Nothing until `customElements.define` runs, when the template is attached
A plain template: its content is inert and is never rendered
An iframe-like sandbox where scripts in the template run on load
A shadow root attached by the parser, with scoped styles and the slot filled
questions.why: Declarative shadow DOM lets the HTML parser attach a shadow root from a `<template shadowrootmode>`, so server-rendered components display with encapsulated styles before any script loads. The element can be upgraded later by a definition that reuses the existing root. It has been supported in every major browser since 2024.
questions.asked: Server-rendering web components used to be impossible, and this is what changed.

questions.q: You deploy a new service worker. Users with the app open in one tab keep getting the old version even after reloading. Why?
choices: Service workers are cached for 24 hours regardless of headers
The new worker is installed but waits until every tab using the old one closes
Reloading bypasses the service worker, so the old HTTP cache is used
The new worker is rejected because its scope matches the old worker's
questions.why: A new service worker installs and then waits while any client is controlled by the old one; a reload does not release it, because the old page stays alive until the new one commits. Apps show an "Update available" prompt and call `skipWaiting()`, or call it on install and accept mixed versions.
questions.asked: The PWA update lifecycle is where most service-worker bugs live, and this waiting phase is its core.

questions.q: After Back, a product page is restored from the back/forward cache and shows a stale cart count. Which listener lets the page refresh it?
choices: `DOMContentLoaded`, which fires again on restoration
`load`, which fires again with `event.persisted` set
`popstate`, which fires for every back navigation
`pageshow`, checking `event.persisted` to spot a restore
questions.why: A bfcache restore brings back the frozen page without reloading it, so `DOMContentLoaded` and `load` do not fire again. `pageshow` fires on every show, and `persisted` is true when the page came from the cache. `popstate` is for same-document history entries.
questions.asked: bfcache gives instant Back navigation, and handling its staleness is the mid-to-senior detail.

questions.q: A router stores its view state in history. What happens here?
choices: It throws a `DataCloneError`: functions cannot be structured-cloned
It works, and the function runs when the user presses Back
It works, but `onBack` is silently dropped from the saved state
It works, and the state is saved as a JSON string in the URL
questions.why: History state is stored with the structured clone algorithm so it can survive reloads and session restores, and functions cannot be cloned, so `pushState` throws. Keep state to plain data (and small), and derive behaviour from it in the `popstate` handler.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know what history state is, which matters when building or debugging routers.

questions.q: The SPA on `https://app.example.com` calls `https://api.example.com` with `credentials: 'include'`. The session cookie is `SameSite=Lax`. Is it sent?
choices: No: `Lax` cookies are only sent on top-level GET navigations
No: any cross-origin request drops `Lax` cookies
Yes: the two hosts are same-site, so `SameSite` does not block it
Yes, but only if the cookie also has `Domain=api.example.com`
questions.why: SameSite compares sites (scheme plus registrable domain), and both hosts are on `example.com`, so the request is same-site even though it is cross-origin. The cookie is sent, provided CORS allows credentials. From `evil.com` it would be cross-site and the `Lax` rule would apply.
questions.asked: Site versus origin is the distinction behind most modern cookie confusion.

questions.q: Every PUT from the SPA triggers an OPTIONS request first, doubling latency. Without changing the request, how can the server reduce this?
choices: Send `Access-Control-Max-Age` so browsers cache the preflight
Send `Cache-Control: max-age=600` on the PUT response itself
Respond to OPTIONS with 204 No Content instead of 200 OK
Add `Connection: keep-alive` to the OPTIONS response
questions.why: `Access-Control-Max-Age` tells the browser how long it may reuse a preflight result for that URL and method set; browsers cap it (Chrome at 2 hours). `Cache-Control` on the real response does not affect preflight caching, and a 200 or 204 makes no difference.
questions.asked: A performance-meets-CORS question; knowing preflights can be cached is the mid-level signal.

questions.q: A live-updates feed uses `EventSource`. The connection drops for ten seconds. What happens without extra code?
choices: The EventSource closes for good and fires `error` once
It reconnects and replays every event the server ever sent
It stops until the page calls `source.reconnect()`
It reconnects, sending `Last-Event-ID` so the server can resume
questions.why: Server-sent events reconnect automatically after a delay the server can set with `retry:`, and if events carried `id:` fields the browser sends the last one in `Last-Event-ID`. The server decides what to replay from it. WebSockets have no built-in reconnect, which is one reason SSE suits one-way feeds.
questions.asked: Comparing SSE with WebSockets comes up in realtime questions, and auto-reconnect is the practical differentiator.

questions.q: In a browser that supports the Navigation API, what does this give a client-side router that `pushState` alone does not?
choices: Server-side rendering of each route before the handler runs
Cross-origin navigations that stay inside the single-page app
One event for links, forms and back/forward, made same-document
Automatic caching of rendered routes in the back/forward cache
questions.why: The `navigate` event fires for every navigation the page can see, and `intercept()` turns it into a same-document one with your handler, so a router no longer needs its own link-click listener plus `popstate`. It also tracks the handler's promise for loading state and scroll/focus handling. Cross-origin navigations cannot be intercepted.
questions.asked: Knowing the modern platform replacement for hand-rolled routing is a strong signal of current knowledge.

questions.q: An editor sends the whole 300 KB draft with `fetch(..., { keepalive: true })` when the page is hidden. Why does the request fail?
choices: `keepalive` requests are limited to about 64 KB of body in total
`keepalive` only works with the GET method, never with POST
`keepalive` requests are blocked on HTTPS pages for privacy
`keepalive` needs a service worker to be registered first
questions.why: To stop pages leaving large uploads running after they close, browsers cap the combined body size of in-flight `keepalive` requests (and `sendBeacon`) at about 64 KB. Save drafts incrementally while the page is open and use the unload-time request only for a small final delta.
questions.asked: Autosave-on-exit is a common feature, and the size limit is the production gotcha.
